---
description: What an implementation of the Criteria aspect of /skill must contain - how a skill's Criteria are drafted, checked, repaired, and improved.
tags: [skill-design, aspect, criteria]
interface:
  cardinality: one
  version: 1
  sections:
    - {heading: Draft, required: true, holds: How create writes a skill's Criteria from its approved Intent.}
    - {heading: Criteria, required: true, holds: The aspect's own checks on a skill's Criteria, each with an ID and how it is decided.}
    - {heading: Fix, holds: How to repair each failed check.}
    - {heading: Enhance, holds: What to look for when suggesting a better set of Criteria.}
---

## Receives

The skill's approved Intent, and the sources it cites when `/skillify` wrote the description.

## Produces

The skill's Criteria: boolean statements about the skill's result, each with an ID `C<n>`, written where the agent
running the skill reads them before it reports done. Verification writes one rubric per Criteria ID, so the IDs never
change meaning; a removed criterion retires its ID.

## Check format

Each item under `## Criteria` is one check: `- **<ID>** [<how>] <statement>`. `<ID>` is `CRI-<n>`. `<how>` is
`script` when a script decides it from the files alone, `read` when an agent decides it by reading the skill, or `run`
when only running the skill decides it, which `/skill check` reports as not checked and points to `test`.

---
description: The default Criteria aspect of /skill - a skill's Criteria as a Done when list of boolean statements about its result.
tags: [skill-design, aspect, criteria]
implements: skill-design.aspects.criteria@1
check-script: ../skills/skill/scripts/check-criteria.mjs
---

## Draft

1. From the Intent, list what must be true of the result when the job is done well. Ask what a reviewer of the result
   would reject, and what the author corrected last time the job was done by hand.
2. Write each as one statement that is true or false of the result: "every merged pull request appears once", not
   "summarize the pull requests well". Name the thing in the result a reader looks at.
3. Keep only what a reader can decide from the result and the case's inputs, without seeing how the agent worked. A
   rule about how to work belongs in the steps, not here.
4. Give each an ID, `C1`, `C2`, and so on, in the order a reviewer would check them.
5. Write them as the last section of `SKILL.md`, `## Done when`, one per line: `- **C1.** <statement>`. Add one line
   before the list: "Before reporting done, check each of these against the result. Report any that fails."
6. Show the list to the author. Three to seven criteria is usual; more than ten usually means two jobs.

## Criteria

- **CRI-1** [script] `SKILL.md` has a `## Done when` section with at least one item.
- **CRI-2** [script] Each item starts with an ID `C<n>`, and no ID appears twice.
- **CRI-3** [read] Each item is true or false of the result, not a goal or a quality ("clear", "good", "well").
- **CRI-4** [read] Each item can be decided from the result and the case's inputs alone.
- **CRI-5** [read] Together the items cover the result the Intent names; nothing the Intent promises is left without
  a criterion.
- **CRI-6** [read] No item restates a rule another aspect already checks, such as the description's length.

## Fix

- CRI-1: draft the section as in Draft, and ask the author to approve it.
- CRI-2: number the items in order; a duplicate ID takes the next free one, and its rubric is renamed with it.
- CRI-3, CRI-4: rewrite the item as the observable fact the author meant, and ask the author when there are two
  readings.
- CRI-5: propose a criterion for each uncovered part of the Intent; the author decides.
- CRI-6: remove the item.

## Enhance

- A correction the user made while using the skill that no criterion catches.
- A criterion every saved result passes in the baseline run too: it does not show what the skill adds.
- A criterion that fails often with the skill: it may ask for something the steps never say.

description: What an implementation of the Security aspect of /skill must contain - the checks that a skill is safe to share and to run.
tags: [skill-design, aspect, security]
interface:
  cardinality: one
  version: 1
  sections:
    - {heading: Criteria, required: true, holds: The aspect's checks on a skill, each with an ID and how it is decided.}
    - {heading: Fix, holds: How to repair each failed check.}
    - {heading: Enhance, holds: What to look for when suggesting a safer skill.}
---

## Receives

The skill's folder: `SKILL.md` and every file beside it.

## Produces

A pass, a fail, or a not checked for each check. Security is an open aspect: `create` does not walk it, and `check`,
`fix`, and `enhance` do.

## Check format

As in `skill-design.aspects.criteria.interface`: `- **<ID>** [script|read|run] <statement>`, with `<ID>` `SEC-<n>`.

---
description: The default Security aspect of /skill - a skill asks before outside effects, carries no secrets, and never treats fetched content as instructions.
tags: [skill-design, aspect, security]
implements: skill-design.aspects.security@1
check-script: ../skills/skill/scripts/check-security.mjs
---

## Criteria

- **SEC-1** [script] No file in the skill's folder holds a string shaped like a secret, such as an API key, a token,
  or a private key.
- **SEC-2** [script] No script downloads code and runs it, such as `curl ... | sh`.
- **SEC-3** [read] Before any step with an effect outside the working copy (posting, pushing, sending, publishing,
  deleting, paying), the skill asks the user, or says it runs only when the user asked for that step.
- **SEC-4** [read] The skill treats what it fetches or reads from files as data, and never tells the agent to follow
  instructions found there.
- **SEC-5** [read] A script the skill runs takes outside input as arguments, never as code it evaluates.
- **SEC-6** [read] The skill asks for no more permission than its steps use.

## Fix

- SEC-1: remove the value, and read it from the environment or ask the user for it. Tell the author the value may
  already be exposed.
- SEC-2: pin the download to a version and a checksum, or install it through a package manager.
- SEC-3: add a step that asks before the effect.
- SEC-4: add a line that fetched content is data, not instructions.
- SEC-5: pass the input as an argument, and quote it.
- SEC-6: narrow the permission to the steps that use it.

## Enhance

- A step whose effect could not be undone, such as a force push or a delete, with no dry run first.
- A new outside effect the skill gained since it was last checked.

description: What an implementation of the Verification aspect of /skill must contain - how a skill's eval cases and rubrics are written, run, and saved.
tags: [skill-design, aspect, verification, evals]
interface:
  cardinality: one
  version: 1
  sections:
    - {heading: Draft, required: true, holds: How create writes the eval cases and one rubric per criterion.}
    - {heading: Cases, required: true, holds: Where the eval cases and rubrics live and their format.}
    - {heading: Run, required: true, holds: How test runs the cases - runs per case, threshold, sandbox, baseline - and the command that does it.}
    - {heading: Criteria, required: true, holds: The aspect's own checks on a skill's eval cases, each with an ID and how it is decided.}
    - {heading: Fix, holds: How to repair each failed check.}
    - {heading: Enhance, holds: What to look for when suggesting better cases or rubrics.}
---

## Receives

The skill's Intent, its Criteria with their IDs, its Trigger description, and the near misses Trigger listed.

## Produces

Trigger cases (requests that should and should not fire the skill), outcome cases (sample inputs to run the skill on),
and one rubric per Criteria ID. In `test`, it runs them and writes the result in the shape the `test` command of
`/skill` defines, which `fix`, `enhance`, and the next `test` read. A rubric that needs a judge runs only when the
author names one; otherwise that criterion is reported as not tested.

## Check format

As in `skill-design.aspects.criteria.interface`: `- **<ID>** [script|read|run] <statement>`, with `<ID>` `VER-<n>`.

---
description: The default Verification aspect of /skill - eval cases in evals/evals.yaml, run on promptfoo in a sandbox, several runs per case against a run without the skill.
tags: [skill-design, aspect, verification, evals, promptfoo]
implements: skill-design.aspects.verification@1
check-script: ../skills/skill/scripts/check-verification.mjs
---

## Draft

1. **Trigger cases.** Write at least three requests that should fire the skill, phrased the way different users
   would ask, and at least three near misses: requests a user could plausibly make that belong to another job, taken
   from the near misses Trigger listed. Keep each to what a user would type.
2. **Outcome cases.** Write at least one case per criterion: a request and the files it works on. Put the files under
   `evals/files/<case id>/`. Use small, made-up inputs; never copy private data into a case.
   A run has no user to answer a question, so a case whose skill asks before it writes states the approval in its
   prompt, such as "I approve writing it; don't ask again".
3. **Rubrics.** For each Criteria ID, write the checks that decide it from a run's output. Prefer a deterministic
   check. Use `judge` only when no deterministic check decides the criterion, and say so to the author.
4. Mark a case `effects: outside` when running it would reach past the sandbox, such as posting to GitHub. It is not
   run.
5. Show the cases and rubrics to the author before writing them.

## Cases

The skill's `evals/evals.yaml`:

```yaml
runs: 3            # runs per case; optional
threshold: 2       # runs a criterion must pass out of `runs`; optional
timeout: 300       # seconds one run may take; optional, 300 by default
concurrency: 4     # runs at once; optional; below half the hardware threads by default, never above it
trigger:
  - prompt: write release notes for the last release
    expect: fire
  - prompt: summarize this pull request for a reviewer
    expect: skip
outcome:
  - id: two-prs
    prompt: write release notes for the changes in this folder
    files: files/two-prs      # copied into the run's folder; optional
    criteria: [C1, C2]        # optional; every criterion by default
    effects: outside          # optional; the case is not run
    checks:                   # optional; per-case checks that replace rubrics.<ID> for this case
      C2:
        - contains: "no merge commits"
rubrics:
  C1:
    - contains: "## Release notes"
  C2:
    - not-regex: "Merge (pull request|branch)"
  C3:
    - judge: Pass when every pull request title in the input appears exactly once.
```

A rubric is a list of checks; a run passes the criterion when every check passes. The checks are `contains`,
`not-contains`, `regex`, `not-regex`, `file-exists` and `file-contains` (`{path, text}`) on the run's folder,
`script` (a command run in the run's folder that exits 0 to pass), and `judge` (a statement a named judge decides).

A rubric judges every outcome case that tests its criterion by the same checks. When a case needs different checks, give
it `checks`, a mapping of criterion ID to a list of checks of the same kinds. For that case, a criterion listed in
`checks` uses those checks instead of `rubrics.<ID>`:

```yaml
outcome:
  - id: find-none
    prompt: Is there a reference about deploy checklists?
    files: files/repo
    criteria: [C6]
    checks:
      C6:
        - regex: "\\b([Nn]o|[Nn]othing|[Nn]one)\\b.{0,40}\\b(match|reference|found)"
```

A criterion counts as having a rubric (VER-3) when it has `rubrics.<ID>` or when every outcome case that tests it has
`checks.<ID>`. An ID in `checks` that is not a Criteria ID fails VER-3.

## Run

Run `test <skill folder>` with the `/skill` command, as its Run the command says. It runs promptfoo at a pinned version
through `npx`, so the first run downloads it. Add `--judge <model>` only when the author named a judge, `--baseline
<folder>` to compare with another version instead of a run without the skill, and `--model <model>` to choose the model
each run uses. It saves the result, prints it, and exits 1 when a case or a criterion fails. Each run's result stays local (the
results folder ignores itself). Each save keeps `latest.json` and the 5 most recent past results of the skill, and deletes
older ones. It also deletes the results of any other skill whose recorded skill folder no longer exists, and leaves a
result with no recorded folder alone. Add `--accept` to also keep the result as the skill's expected result,
`evals/expected.json`, which `changed` compares with in later runs; `skill accept <folder>` does the same with the last
saved result without running. `expected.json` is optional, and the checks do not require it. Each run makes model calls:
say so before the first run in a session.

- The default is `runs: 3` and `threshold: 2`. A criterion passes when it passes in at least `threshold` runs.
- Each run starts in a fresh copy of the case's files, which is a git repository with those files committed (a local
  throwaway identity; the installed skill is excluded from `git status`), so a skill or a `script` check can use git. It has no user configuration, memory, or user-level skills, and
  only the skill under test installed, through promptfoo's Claude Agent SDK provider and Claude Code's own login. Web
  tools are off, and each run stops at 20 turns or $0.50.
- A skill developed in a plugin (a folder above it holds `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, and the skill is in that
  plugin's skills folder) runs inside a copy of that plugin from the working copy, loaded through the provider's
  `plugins` option, so it reads the plugin's references and other skills as an install would. It is then called
  `<plugin>:<skill>`. The baseline loads the same copy without the skill, or with the `--baseline` version in its place.
  The copy leaves out `node_modules` and `.git`.
- Each run records every skill it calls in `.skill-test/skill-calls.jsonl`, one JSON line `{"skill", "args"}` per call,
  excluded from `git status`. A `script` check reads it to decide what a skill handed to another, such as the
  description a skill passed to `/skill create`.
- Each run's `HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` point at fresh empty folders, so a skill's own CLI run
  through Bash finds no user references or plugins, no installed Claude Code plugin is loaded, and the Bash tool sources
  no user shell snapshot. Claude Code's login still works because `CLAUDE_SECURESTORAGE_CONFIG_DIR` points at the real
  Claude config folder (or the one already set), where Claude Code reads and refreshes its own credentials; no credential
  is copied or linked, and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` pass through when set. If a Claude Code
  version ignores that variable, each run fails with "Not logged in" and counts as not run. On macOS the real config
  folder is kept instead, since the keychain entry is named after it, so plugins and the shell snapshot still leak
  there. A skill that reads a file by its absolute path under the real home still reaches it. The folder of the `node`
  running the test goes first on `PATH`, since a version manager's shim reads its config from the home folder; another
  tool a shim provides may not run.
- Each case runs twice over: once with the skill and once without it, which is the baseline.
- At most `concurrency` runs go at once: by default the largest number below half the machine's hardware threads (7 of
  16), and at least 1. A larger `concurrency` is lowered to that.
- `skill test <folder> --case <id>` (repeatable) runs only the named cases, outcome IDs or `trigger-<n>`. The result is
  marked partial, is compared with the expected result for those cases only, and is never saved as the expected result.
- A run stops after `timeout` seconds (300 by default, set in `evals.yaml`); its Claude process and the shells and commands it started are killed, and it counts as not run with the reason `time limit`. A process stuck in uninterruptible disk sleep cannot be killed; the test stops waiting for it and goes on.
- A run that errors or hits its time or token limit counts as not run, never as a pass.
- In a run, one shell command stops after 30 seconds unless the model asks for longer, and after 2 minutes at most;
  it is stopped, not moved to the background, so a runaway command such as `find /` costs seconds, not the whole run.
  A skill under test cannot start a background command.
- A trigger case runs only with the skill. It passes when the skill fired (`expect: fire`) or did not (`expect: skip`) in at least `threshold`
  runs. A trigger run is cut short: it ends at the first skill the model calls, counting as fired only when that is the skill under test, or after three turns, so it does not go on to do the whole job. Running out of those turns is not an error.

## Criteria

- **VER-1** [script] `evals/evals.yaml` exists and follows the format in Cases.
- **VER-2** [script] It has at least three `fire` and three `skip` trigger cases.
- **VER-3** [script] Every Criteria ID has a rubric, and every rubric names a Criteria ID.
- **VER-4** [script] Every `files` folder an outcome case names exists.
- **VER-5** [script] `threshold` is between 1 and `runs`.
- **VER-6** [read] Each `skip` case is a request a user could plausibly make that belongs to another job, not an
  unrelated one.
- **VER-7** [read] Each rubric decides its criterion, not something easier that happens to go with it.
- **VER-8** [read] No case holds private data, such as real names, tokens, or customer text.

## Fix

- VER-1 to VER-5: write or correct the file as Draft and Cases say.
- VER-6: replace the case with a near miss Trigger listed, or ask the author for one.
- VER-7: rewrite the rubric, and use `judge` only when no deterministic check decides the criterion.
- VER-8: replace the data with made-up data of the same shape.

## Enhance

- A trigger miss or a wrong result seen while the skill was used: add it as a case.
- A case that passes with and without the skill alike: it does not show what the skill adds.
- A `judge` rubric that a deterministic check could replace.

name: asset
description: Use this skill when listing, reading, adding, changing, or deleting the static files in a skill's assets/ folder, such as templates, schemas, or JSON data a skill points to by path.
---

# Asset

An **asset** is a static file in a skill's `assets/` folder: a template, a schema, a lookup table, a JSON permission list. Two kinds of work:

- **By path**: manage the files themselves. No tiers, no merging.
- **By name**: load a file the way a reference loads, so a plugin, the project, or the user can override which file a skill uses by placing its own. The managed, project (`.agents/assets/`), user (`~/.agents/assets/`), and plugin tiers read `assets/` folders, and the skill's own `assets/<name>.<ext>` is the default. The highest tier holding the name answers with the file as written. Nothing merges or extends, Markdown included: frontmatter in an asset is just text. Choosing among plugins is a selection, a one-line `<name>.select` file.

For a Markdown document layered across tiers, use the `reference` skill.

## Route

| The request | Run |
| --- | --- |
| see which assets a skill holds | `list` |
| read a text asset | `show <path>` |
| add a new asset | `create <path>` |
| start an override from an existing asset, to edit | `create <name> --copy <plugin\|default\|project\|user> --scope project\|user --default <skill folder>` |
| change an existing asset | `update <path>` |
| remove an asset | `delete <path>` |
| read the asset a skill loads by name, after overrides | `load <name> --default <skill folder>` |
| see which asset names exist | `names --default <skill folder>` |
| see where an override of a name would go | `where <name> --default <skill folder>` |
| choose which plugin's file, or the skill's own, answers a name | `select <name> <option> --default <skill folder>` |

## Run

Find the skill's source folder in the repository (the directory its `SKILL.md` is in), then run from anywhere:

```sh
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/asset.mjs <mode> [<path>] --skill <skill folder> --root <repository root>
```

- `<path>` is relative to `assets/`, with `/` separators and no `..`, such as `data/rules.json`.
- `create` and `update` take the text with `--content "<text>"` or a local file with `--from <file>`; pass exactly one.
- Never use `npx`, `pnpm dlx`, or any package runner, and never download anything.

`load`, `names`, and `where` read only. `create --copy` never copies from the managed tier: it is policy, a copy would leak it into the repository or home folder and read as in effect when the managed file still wins. If asked, refuse and offer `load` to read it.

Ask the user before `create`, `update`, `delete`, or `select`, and name the file.

To make a skill use a different file, place one of the same name in a higher tier: `.agents/assets/<name>.<ext>` for the project, `~/.agents/assets/<name>.<ext>` for the user. When two plugins hold a name and no tier does, `load` reports it ambiguous and lists the options: run `select <name> <option>` (a plugin name, or `default` for the skill's own file; `--scope user` for yourself, `--clear` to undo), ask for `<plugin>/<name>`, or place the file in a tier. `where <name>` shows the folders. `create` never overwrites and `update` needs the file to exist.

## Read the result

Exit 0 means it did what was asked. Exit 1 is a refusal, and stderr says `error: <code>: <message>`: `exists`, `no-file`, `binary`, or `folder-invalid` (the folder is not a skill folder, or is an installed copy or outside the repository). Exit 2 is misuse: a path that leaves `assets/`, or both or neither of `--content` and `--from`. Report the message; do not retry with a different path to get around it.

`show` prints text only. A binary asset is pointed to by path, not shown.

name: prose-update
description: Use this skill when a section of prose a tool wrote earlier may have been edited by its owner and a newer wording is available, to get recommended updated prose that keeps the owner's sentences. Takes the offered prose, the found prose, and the historic prose.
---

# Update prose

Given a newer wording, the text now in a file, and the wordings the tool retired, recommend the updated text. A script returns the facts that settle most cases. You resolve only what it leaves open. Nothing here writes a file or asks the owner: the calling skill does that with your recommendation.

## Inputs

Exactly three, as text:

1. **Offered prose**: the wording the tool offers now.
2. **Found prose**: the text in the file being updated. It may hold several sections.
3. **Historic prose**: either a history text (entries headed `## Superseded <date> — <reason>`, each wording in a fence) or one or more retired wordings, newest first.

Read no file the caller did not name. If one of the three is missing, say which and stop.

## Run

```sh
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/prose-update.mjs classify --offered-from <file> --found-from <file> --history-from <file> --format json
```

Pass `--offered`, `--found`, or `--history` with the text itself instead of the `-from` form, and `--retired` (repeatable, newest first) in place of a history text. Each of the three takes one form, not both. If the script is missing or cannot run, use `pnpm exec cyber-agentkit prose-update` when the package is a direct dependency, else `npx -y cyber-agentkit@2.2.0 prose-update`, with the same arguments.

An empty offered wording exits 1 with `error: empty-offered`. Report it and stop.

## Read the result

Each part (a heading path and the sentences under it) has an `outcome`:

| Outcome | Recommend |
| --- | --- |
| `up-to-date`, `owners` | the part's `text` as found. Nothing is offered. |
| `update` | the part's `text`, merged by the script: the owner's sentences kept, the offered ones taken. |
| `conflict` | the colliding sentences are in `collisions` (base, found, offered). The part's `text` holds the found sentences there. Resolve by reading intent. |
| `undetermined` | the `reason` says why: `no-history`, `empty-section`, `tied-base`, `no-base`. Resolve by reading intent, or give no recommendation. |

The top-level `text` is the whole document as the script merged it. For `up-to-date`, `owners`, and `update` it is the recommended prose: use it as is and mark no sentence as decided.

## Resolve what the script left open

Only for `conflict` and `undetermined` parts.

- Compare meaning, not wording: is the owner's sentence a rewording of the offered one, or a different point?
- Keep every owner sentence. Drop one only when you mark it `decided` with the reason.
- Mark every sentence you wrote or chose that is not from the found text, the offered wording, or an owner sentence as `decided`, with the reason.
- When you cannot choose, give no recommendation for the part. Name the part and the choice the owner must make.

## Answer

Return the recommended prose, then for each part its outcome, and for each sentence whether it was kept, taken from the offered wording, or decided. Ask the owner a question only for a part that is a `conflict` or `undetermined`, or whose recommendation carries a `decided` sentence.

Save it only after the user approves. Write new wordings so that they only add sentences after the old ones: such a revision merges without collision.

Also use it to migrate reference files left in a version 1 form, or under a name a plugin renamed, as a `reference-legacy-format` or `reference-renamed` warning asks.
---

# Reference

Route the request to one mode, then follow that mode.

A **reference** is a document read by name. Each place that holds a **contribution** to a name is a **tier**:

- the plugins that ship the name, and the loading skill's **default** (`references/<name>.default.md` in its folder). They form the stack, bottom first, in the order `extends` gives.
- `user`: `~/.agents/references/`, for one person in every repository. It applies over the stack.
- `repo`: `.agents/references/` at the repository root, for everyone working in it. It applies over `user`.
- a **project section**: `.agents/references/<name>.md` in a folder below the root. It states only what differs for work in that folder, and follows the main document.
- `managed`: an admin's folder for the running harness. It applies over the main document and over each project section.

Each contribution applies with its `merge`: `patch` (the default) replaces the text a section matches, `combine` adds after it, `replace` drops everything below, and `remove` turns the name off. An **interface** is a contract, declared in a `<id>.interface` reference, that other references implement. What answers a name is the `reference` command's decision. Never decide it by reading tier folders yourself.

## Route

| The request | Mode |
| --- | --- |
| a skill's instructions name references, or an interface's implementations, to load with this skill | [Load](#load) |
| find a reference for a topic, list them, or list an interface's implementations | [Find](#find) |
| read a reference, learn why it composed as it did, where a customization goes, or check it against its interface | [Inspect](#inspect) |
| write a new reference from text the author gives: for the repository, the user, a plugin to ship, or a skill's default; or stub an interface | [Create](#create) |
| edit the user's own reference file in place | [Update](#update) |
| choose what a name builds on, settle an ambiguous name, change what a reference says, or revise a stale one | [Customize](#customize) |
| remove a repo, user, or project-section contribution | [Delete](#delete) |
| bring reference files written for version 1 to the 2.0 form, or rename them as a plugin renamed their names, as a `reference-legacy-format` or `reference-renamed` warning asks | [Migrate](#migrate) |
| make a skill load a reference | [Wire a skill](#wire-a-skill) |

Ask only when the request fits two modes. Otherwise pick one; outside Load, say which. Invoked as `/reference` with no request, run `list` from [Find](#find) and ask what to do with one.

## Run the command

```sh
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/reference.mjs <subcommand> ...
```

`scripts/reference.mjs` is the package's `reference` command bundled into one file; it needs no `node_modules`. It finds the repository root from the working folder. Add `--root <repository root>` only when the working folder is not in the repository. A command that cannot complete exits 1 (or 2 for a usage error) and prints one error value on stdout, with `error` and `code` lines. A warning prints `warning: <code>: <message>` on stderr in text output, and does not change the exit code.

Outside Load, when the script is missing or cannot run, use `pnpm exec cyber-agentkit reference` when the package is a direct dependency, else `npx -y cyber-agentkit@2.2.0 reference`, with the same arguments. Load never falls back to a package runner.

## Load

Load [references/load.md](references/load.md) from this skill's folder and follow it, then return to the caller's work.

## Find

- For a topic, run `search <query>`. If nothing matches, say that nothing matched. Do not guess a name.
- When `search` carries a `count` field, it shows only the best matches. Run it again with `--full` when none of them fits.
- For every reference, run `list`. Add `--trace` for every contribution of each name and its outcome.
- For every name matching a pattern, run `list '<pattern>'`. `*` stands for any run of characters and the rest is literal.
- For the implementations of an interface, run `implementations <id>`. It lists each one a consumer can load, with its pin. Add `--trace` for each one it left out, with why. For a `one` interface it also gives `inUse`, the implementation a load builds on: a pin, or `default`. A family `<prefix>.*` lists every interface under the prefix at once, each as `implementations <id>` lists it.
- When `list` or `search` carries a `defaults` field, say that skills' defaults were not searched, and why.

## Inspect

- To read a reference, run `load <name>`. Add `--metadata` for its composed frontmatter.
- To learn why a name composed as it did, run `load <name> --trace`. Report the stack and what built it, the contribution each section came from, each project section, and each layer that was `shadowed`, `stale`, `not used`, or `not read`, with its reason.
- To check a reference, run `check <name>...`: an interface document against its shape, an implementation against its interface, and every document for defects. With no name, it checks every name and reports every warning `load` would raise. It exits 0; report each entry under `failed` with its check, and each under `warned` with its warnings.
- To learn where a customization goes, run `where <name>`. Add `--default <skill folder>` when a skill loads the name, and `--in <folder>` for a folder's project section. Report each file, who it reaches, and what hides it. A plugin's or a skill's default contribution is read-only; never offer it as a place to write.

## Create

Load [references/create.md](references/create.md) from this skill's folder and follow it.

## Update

Use Update only for a file the user wrote by hand under `.agents/references/` or `~/.agents/references/`.

1. Run `load <name> --trace`. Find the `used` layer for that file.
2. If its trace row records a `request`, it is generated. Never edit it by hand; go to [Customize](#customize).
3. Show the user the change and the path. On approval, edit the file.
4. Run `load <name> --trace` again. The file must be `used`, and `load <name>` must give no `marker-unmatched` warning.

## Customize

Load [references/customize.md](references/customize.md) from this skill's folder and follow it.

## Delete

1. Run `load <name> --trace`. Use the bare name.
2. Choose the place: the repository (the default), the user with `--scope user`, or one folder's project section with `--in <folder>`. An author may also delete from a plugin's or a skill's source folder in this repository with `--plugin` or `--default`. An installed plugin's, a managed, or an installed skill's contribution is never deleted; offer a customization with `merge: remove` through [Customize](#customize) instead.
3. Run `delete <name> --dry-run` with that place's flag. Show the user the path and what will answer the name afterwards, and say so when a selection goes with the file.
4. On approval, run it without `--dry-run`.
5. Run `load <name> --trace` again. The deleted file must be gone from the trace.

## Migrate

Use Migrate for files a customizer or an author wrote: under `.agents/references/` at the root or in a folder below it, under `~/.agents/references/`, or in a plugin's or a skill's source folder in this repository. `migrate` rewrites each version 1 form as its 2.0 form (`merge: merge-sections` is removed, `merge: first-wins` becomes `merge: replace`, `overrides` becomes `extends`, a skill's `references/<name>.md` becomes `<name>.default.md`, a qualified-name override `<plugin>/<name>.md` moves out of its subfolder to `<name>.md` with `extends: [<plugin>]`), and renames each file under a name a plugin renamed. It keeps the body and every other key.

1. Run `migrate`, with the names to limit it to, if any. For a plugin's source folder, add `--plugin <folder>`; for a skill's, add `--default <folder>` and the names the skill loads, since its other files may be its own documents. It prints the plan and writes nothing.
2. If it answers `0 changes`, say so and stop.
3. Show the user every row: the file, its tier, and the change. Say plainly that each `user` row edits a file in their home folder that no git history restores. For a `manual` row, show why; for a selection or a qualified-name override in a project folder, offer the `customize` command it gives, through [Customize](#customize).
4. With no user present, write nothing, and report the plan.
5. Only after the user approves, run the same command with `--write`.
6. Run `check` with the changed names. Report any `reference-legacy-format` or `reference-renamed` left, with its file.

## Wire a skill

A skill never runs the command itself. It carries one load line naming this skill and its package. Copy the line from the `README.md` in this skill's folder and replace the example names:

```text
Load `<name>` and `<name>` with the `reference` skill of `cyber-agentkit`.
Load the implementations of the `<id>` interface with the `reference` skill of `cyber-agentkit`.
```

A skill written for one harness may add that harness's typed form after the skill's name; the README lists each one. The skill may ship its own default of a name at `references/<name>.default.md` in its folder. Load adds it below every other contribution, and reads it on its own only when the command cannot run. A copy at `references/<name>.md` is not read as a default.

## Rules

- **Only Create, Update, Customize, Delete, and Migrate write.** Load writes only a pick the user made for an ambiguous name. Find, Inspect, and Wire a skill change no reference file.
- **Never edit, move, rename, or delete a reference an installed plugin or skill ships, or a managed one, not even to migrate it.** Customize it instead. Its callers load it by name.
- **Never edit a generated document by hand.** Customize it again with its request.
- **Write only what the user approves.** Show the file and its path before you write or delete it. A request to create a reference from text the user gives is its approval: write it, then show the file and its path. With no user present, write nothing.

## Done when

Before reporting done, check each of these against the result. Report any that fails.

- **C1.** A file written or deleted by Create, Update, Customize, Delete, or Migrate is under `.agents/references/` at the root or in a folder below it, under `~/.agents/references/`, or, for Create and Delete, in a plugin's or a skill's source folder in this repository.
- **C2.** No file in an installed plugin or skill, or in a managed folder, changed.
- **C3.** The file and its path were shown to the user before the write or the delete, or, for a Create from text the user gave, right after the write. A delete also said what answers the name afterwards. A migrate showed every row of its plan.
- **C4.** After a write, `load <name> --trace` reports the written file as `used`, or names what hides it.
- **C5.** A written reference that declares `implements` passes `check <name>`.
- **C6.** A Load, Find, or Inspect answer matches what the `reference` command printed. A search that matched nothing says so and names no reference.

# Skill

Route the request to one command, load that command's file from this skill's folder, and follow it. Every command
works through the aspects below.

## Commands

| Command | Use it when | Instructions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `help` | the author wants to know what each command does, or which one fits | [references/help.md](references/help.md) |
| `create [description]` | the author wants a new skill for a job they describe | [references/create.md](references/create.md) |
| `check [skill]` | the author wants to know whether a skill as written meets each aspect, without running it | [references/check.md](references/check.md) |
| `test [skill]` | the author wants the skill's evals run: does it fire on the right requests, and does its result meet its Criteria | [references/test.md](references/test.md) |
| `fix [skill]` | `check` or `test` found failures to repair | [references/fix.md](references/fix.md) |
| `enhance [skill] [prompt]` | the skill passes `check`, and the author wants it better, from its use or their own request | [references/enhance.md](references/enhance.md) |
| `customize [aspect]` | the author wants to see or change which implementation each aspect uses, or how much each command applies on its own | [references/customize.md](references/customize.md) |

Take an explicit command first. Otherwise read the intent from the request; if it fits two commands, ask which. With
no request, follow `help`.

## Aspects

An aspect is one step of designing a skill: what it receives, what it produces, and the checks on its output. The
core aspects, in the order `create` walks them, are Intent, Criteria, Shape, Trigger, then Verification. Every other
aspect is open: `check`, `fix`, and `enhance` use it, and `create` does not walk it.

Intent, Shape, and Trigger are written below. Criteria, Verification, and every open aspect are references a team can
swap. Load `skill-design.aspects.criteria` and `skill-design.aspects.verification` with the `reference` skill of
`cyber-agentkit`. For the open aspects, use that skill's Find mode to list `skill-design.aspects.*`, and load each name
it lists other than `criteria`, `verification`, and names ending `.interface`.

When the load reports that a chosen implementation is missing and the default answered instead, tell the author which
aspect fell back and which implementation was missing.

Each aspect's checks are listed as `- **<ID>** [<how>] <statement>`. `script` means a script decides it from the files
alone, `read` means you decide it by reading the skill, and `run` means only running the skill decides it: `check`
reports it as not checked and points to `test`.

### Intent

Produces the opening paragraph of the skill's `README.md`, right under its `#` title: the one job the skill does, who
asks for it, and the result it hands back. It may also name the nearest job the skill does not do, when readers are
likely to confuse the two. It is for the people who keep the skill.
`SKILL.md` carries no Intent paragraph: its description, steps, and `## Done when` already tell the agent the job and
the result.

**Draft.** From the author's description (which `/skillify` may have written from work already done), write the
paragraph in four sentences or fewer. Ask the author when the job could be read two ways, and when the result is
not named.

- **INT-1** [read] The opening paragraph of `README.md` names one job and the result the skill hands back.
- **INT-3** [read] Nothing in the body works on a job the Intent does not name.

**Fix.** Changing the Intent is the author's decision: propose the change and ask, at every autonomy level.

### Shape

Produces the skill's folder layout: what stays in `SKILL.md`, and what moves to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.

**Draft.** Keep everything in `SKILL.md` while its body stays under 500 lines. Move to `references/` text read only on
some paths, such as one command's steps, and link each file from the step that needs it. Move to `scripts/` any step a
program does the same way every time, such as parsing or validating a file. Propose the layout to the author.

- **SHP-1** [script] The `SKILL.md` body is at most 500 lines.
- **SHP-2** [script] Every file the body links exists, and every file under `references/` is linked from the body or
  from a file it links, except a reference default (`<name>.default.md`), which is loaded by name.
- **SHP-3** [read] A step that applies fixed rules to data (filtering, sorting, grouping, counting, or formatting) is a
  script, not prose, however few its rules. Judgment, such as choosing what to say, stays prose.
- **SHP-4** [read] Each file under `references/` is read only on some paths; text every run needs is in `SKILL.md`.

**Fix.** Move the text or the step as Draft says, and update the links.

### Trigger

Produces the `description` in the skill's front matter, and the near misses Verification turns into `skip` cases.

**Draft.** Start with "Use this skill when", then name the job in the words users type, with two or three phrasings.
Say nothing about when not to use it. List three or more near misses: requests a user could plausibly make that
belong to the nearest other jobs. They go to Verification as `skip` cases, not into the description.

- **TRG-1** [read] The description says when to use the skill, in words a user would type.
- **TRG-3** [read] It describes when to use the skill, not how the skill works.
- **TRG-4** [run] The skill fires on the requests it should and not on near misses.

**Fix.** Rewrite the description as Draft says; for TRG-4, use the failed cases in the `test` result.

## Run the command

```sh
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/skill.mjs <subcommand> ...
```

`scripts/skill.mjs` is the package's `skill` command bundled into one file. When it is missing or cannot run, use
`pnpm exec cyber-agentkit skill` when the package is a direct dependency, else `npx -y cyber-agentkit@2.2.0 skill`,
with the same arguments.

## Autonomy

Load `skill-design.autonomy` with the `reference` skill of `cyber-agentkit`. It sets one level per command:

- `ask`: propose each item; the author decides.
- `apply-safe`: apply each change after which `check` and `test` pass with no criterion worse than before; ask about
  the rest, or report them when no author is present.
- `apply`: apply every change, and report each one.

A decision only the author can make (changing the Intent, what a skill generalizes over, an aspect the description says
nothing about) is asked at every level; with no author present, report it as not applied. A level set for `check` or
`test` has no effect: say so. A level that names no known value leaves the command at its default: say so.

## Rules

- When the skill named cannot be found, stop, say where you looked, and write nothing.
- A skill that `create` writes meets the Agent Skills specification: `name` is 1 to 64 lowercase letters,
  digits, and hyphens and matches the folder; `description` is 1 to 1024 characters.
- Run no judge unless the author names one.
- In an interactive run that found failures, end `check` and `test` by offering `fix`. Change nothing unless the author
  accepts. With no author present, make no offer.
- Never edit a skill that came from an installed plugin without saying first that a plugin update will overwrite the
  change.

## Done when

Before reporting done, check each of these against the result. Report any that fails.

- **C1.** When the skill named cannot be found, the reply says where it looked, and no file changed.
- **C2.** `check` changed no file.
- **C3.** `check` reports no failure on a skill that meets every aspect, and names each check a skill fails, by its ID.
- **C4.** `create` on a name that already exists left that skill unchanged and pointed to `check`, `fix`, and `enhance`.
- **C5.** At `ask`, `create` wrote nothing the author had not approved.
- **C6.** After `fix`, the checks it repaired pass a fresh `check`.
- **C7.** `fix` changed no part of the skill that no failure named, and no file outside it.
- **C8.** `help` named every command and `/skillify`, and changed no file.
- **C9.** `customize` showed each aspect with the implementation in use, and changed no file the author had not picked.

# Skillify

Write a description of a skill from work already done, then run `/skill create` on it. The sources show what was
done, not what the skill should do: the author decides that when `create` asks them to approve the Intent.

## 1. Read the sources

1. The sources are what the prompt names: a document, another skill, or past sessions, such as "the sessions of the
   last week". With no prompt, the source is this session's work. The prompt can also say which job in the sources to
   capture.
2. If a named source cannot be read, stop and name it. If this session holds no work and the prompt names no other
   source, say there is nothing to skillify, point to `/skill create`, and write nothing.
3. Never change a source.

## 2. Find the job

1. One source holding more than one job, with the prompt naming none: propose one skill per job, and build none until
   the author picks.
2. Several sources not sharing one job: propose one skill per job found in more than one source, name the jobs found
   in only one, and build none until the author picks.
3. Otherwise the job is the one the sources share.

## 3. Decide what varies

- **Several sources:** the steps every source shares are the skill's steps. Each value that differs between them,
  such as the repository, the version, or the target, is an input.
- **One source:** propose what would differ on the next run, and make each of those an input.

## 4. Write the description

Answer each question `create` asks the author, from the sources, generalized over step 3:

- **Job and result:** the job the sources did and the result it handed back.
- **Corrections:** what the author corrected or rejected, and the checks the sources ran on the result.
- **Fixed steps:** the steps done the same way every time.
- **Asking words:** the words the author used to ask for the job.
- **Cases:** the requests and inputs a case could use, rewritten as made-up cases of the same shape.
- **Generalizes over:** the inputs step 3 found.

After each answer, name the part of the source it came from, such as a section of a document or a turn of a session.
Leave out an answer the sources do not hold: `create` asks the author for it.

Check each fact a source states about the repository, such as a path, a file count, or a command, against the
repository now. Where it no longer holds, use what holds now and name the difference.

## 5. Run create

Run `/skill create` (the `skill` skill of `cyber-agentkit`) with the description as its argument, at once, without
asking the author first. `create` acts at its own autonomy level; this skill has none.

## Done when

Before reporting done, check each of these against the result. Report any that fails.

- **C1.** No source changed.
- **C2.** `/skill create` ran with the description, and nothing asked the author before it.
- **C3.** The description states the job and its result, the corrections, the fixed steps, and the asking words, for
  each of them the sources hold.
- **C4.** Each answer in the description names the part of a source it came from.
- **C5.** The description states what the skill generalizes over; with several sources, its steps are those every
  source shares, and each value that differs is named as an input.
- **C6.** Each fact a source states about the repository that no longer holds is replaced by what holds now, with the
  difference named.
- **C7.** A source that could not be read, a session with nothing to skillify, or sources holding more than one job
  ended without running `create` or writing a file, and said why.

# cyber-agentkit

[![license: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](https://github.com/cyber-uni/cyber-agentkit/blob/main/LICENSE)

An agent-harness-agnostic toolkit. It provides the fundamental features agent tools need and makes
each one work the same way across harnesses:

- **Harness knowledge.** Detect which harness is running, and query what it holds: managed-policy
  locations, plugin storage, installed and enabled plugins, skill naming and directories, and how to
  run it headless.
- **Plugin dependencies.** Check which plugins another plugin needs against what the harness has.
- **Reference documents.** Resolve the named Markdown documents an agent reads on demand.
- **Worktrees.** Lease git worktrees to concurrent agent sessions.

It depends on no other agent tool, so any of them can build on it.

**Status: pre-release.** Every fact this library encodes rests on
[`.research/harness-detection`](https://github.com/cyber-uni/cyber-agentkit/tree/main/.research/harness-detection).

## Detect the harness

It detects Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, GitHub Copilot CLI, OpenCode, Kilo Code, Gemini CLI, Qwen
Code, GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Cline, Crush, OpenHands, and the Auggie CLI.

```ts
import { detectHarness } from 'cyber-agentkit'

const result = detectHarness()
// {
//   harness: 'claude-code',
//   candidates: ['claude-code'],
//   evidence: [
//     { harness: 'claude-code', signal: 'CLAUDECODE', research: 'E-CC-D1', description: '…' },
//     { harness: 'claude-code', signal: 'CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION', research: 'E-CC-D3', description: '…' },
//   ],
// }
```

Detection reads environment variables that each harness sets on the processes it spawns:

| Harness | Detected from |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `CLAUDECODE=1` with `CLAUDE_CODE_CHILD_SESSION=1` or `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` |
| Cursor | `CURSOR_AGENT=1`, or `CURSOR_VERSION` with `CURSOR_PROJECT_DIR` in hooks |
| Codex | `CODEX_THREAD_ID` |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | `COPILOT_CLI=1`, `COPILOT_AGENT_SESSION_ID`, or `COPILOT_PLUGIN_ROOT` in hooks |
| OpenCode | `OPENCODE=1` with `OPENCODE_PID` |
| Kilo Code | `KILO=1` with `KILO_PID` |
| Gemini CLI | `GEMINI_CLI=1` |
| Qwen Code | `QWEN_CODE=1` |
| GitHub Copilot in VS Code | `COPILOT_AGENT=1` |
| Cline | `CLINE_ACTIVE=true`, set by the VS Code extension only |
| Crush | `CRUSH=1` |
| OpenHands | `AI_AGENT=openhands`, or `OPENHANDS_EVENT_TYPE` with `OPENHANDS_PROJECT_DIR` in hooks |
| Auggie CLI | `AUGMENT_HOOK_EVENT` with `AUGMENT_PROJECT_DIR`, in hooks only |

It reports `unknown` instead of guessing:

- when no harness matches, including `CLAUDECODE=1` on its own, which IDE extensions also set;
- when more than one harness matches, as when one harness runs inside another's shell. The matches
  are listed in `candidates`;
- for `AGENT` and `AI_AGENT`, which several vendors set (only the exact value `AI_AGENT=openhands`
  counts), and for `OPENCODE=1` alone, which Kilo Code, an OpenCode fork, also sets;
- in contexts where a harness sets nothing of its own: Codex, Gemini CLI, and Qwen Code hooks, Qwen
  Code, Crush, OpenHands, and Auggie MCP servers, Auggie shell commands, OpenHands CLI 1.16.0 shell
  commands (its SDK predates `AI_AGENT=openhands`), and the Cline CLI;
- for harnesses with no verified signal, such as Goose, Antigravity, Rovo Dev, Kiro, Amp, Factory
  Droid, Devin Desktop, and Warp. The research records why for each one.

Pass `{ env }` to inspect an environment other than `process.env`.

## Managed policy

```ts
import { managedPolicyLocations } from 'cyber-agentkit'

managedPolicyLocations('claude-code', { platform: 'linux' })
// [
//   { kind: 'server', location: 'claude.ai admin console or a self-hosted Claude apps gateway', … },
//   { kind: 'file', location: '/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json', … },
//   { kind: 'directory', location: '/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.d', … },
//   { kind: 'file', location: '/etc/claude-code/managed-mcp.json', … },
// ]
```

`kind` is `file` or `directory` for what a caller can read from disk, `macos-managed-preferences`
or `windows-registry` for MDM delivery, and `server` for policy held by the vendor or the
organization. A `server` entry means the local files are not the whole policy.

## Plugin storage

```ts
import { pluginStorage } from 'cyber-agentkit'

pluginStorage('codex')
// {
//   harness: 'codex',
//   configDir: '/home/me/.codex',
//   locations: [
//     { kind: 'plugin-cache', path: '/home/me/.codex/plugins/cache', … },
//     { kind: 'enabled-record', path: '/home/me/.codex/config.toml', … },
//   ],
// }
```

Paths are computed, not checked, so a location may not exist until the first plugin is installed.
Cursor has no `enabled-record`: no file records which of its plugins are enabled.

## Enabled plugins

```ts
import { enabledPlugins } from 'cyber-agentkit'

const result = await enabledPlugins('claude-code')
// {
//   harness: 'claude-code',
//   supported: true,
//   plugins: [{ id: 'my-plugin@my-marketplace', enabled: true, scope: 'project', source: '/repo/.claude/settings.json' }],
//   sources: [{ scope: 'managed', path: '/etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json', found: false }, …],
//   unread: ['server-managed settings (claude.ai admin console or a self-hosted Claude apps gateway)', …],
//   research: ['E-CC-P3', …],
// }
```

| Harness | Files read, highest precedence first |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code | managed `managed-settings.json`, `.claude/settings.local.json`, `.claude/settings.json`, `<config dir>/settings.json` |
| Codex | `<config dir>/config.toml` |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | managed `managed-settings.json`, `.github/copilot/settings.local.json`, `.github/copilot/settings.json`, `<config dir>/settings.json` |
| Cursor, OpenCode, Kilo Code, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Copilot in VS Code, Cline, Crush, OpenHands, Auggie CLI | none: `supported` is `false` |

Only plugins with an explicit entry are reported. A plugin with no entry falls back to a default
this package does not know. When `unread` is not empty, MDM or server-managed policy can still
override the answer.

## Installed plugins

```ts
import { enabledPlugins, installedPlugins } from 'cyber-agentkit'

const installed = await installedPlugins('claude-code')
// {
//   harness: 'claude-code',
//   supported: true,
//   plugins: [{ id: 'my-plugin@my-marketplace', path: '/home/me/.claude/plugins/cache/my-marketplace/my-plugin/1.0.0', version: '1.0.0', scope: 'user', research: ['E-CC-P2'] }],
//   unresolved: [],
//   sources: [{ path: '/home/me/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json', found: true }],
//   unread: [],
//   research: ['E-CC-P2'],
// }

// The folder of each enabled plugin:
const enabled = new Set((await enabledPlugins('claude-code')).plugins.filter((p) => p.enabled).map((p) => p.id))
const folders = installed.plugins.filter((p) => enabled.has(p.id)).map((p) => p.path)
```

| Harness | Read from | Folder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `<config dir>/plugins/installed_plugins.json` | `installPath`; one entry per scope a plugin is installed at |
| Codex | `<config dir>/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>/` | `local` if present, else the highest version, as Codex picks it |
| GitHub Copilot CLI | `<config dir>/config.json` `installedPlugins` | `cache_path`; a direct install's `id` is its bare name |
| Cursor, OpenCode, Kilo Code, Gemini CLI, Qwen Code, Copilot in VS Code, Cline, Crush, OpenHands, Auggie CLI | none: `supported` is `false` | — |

`unresolved` lists Codex plugins whose cache mixes semver and non-semver version folders, where the
folder Codex picks depends on its sort. Copilot CLI loads plugins from a marketplace added by local
path in place, without an install record, so they appear in `unread` instead.

## Plugin dependencies

Only Claude Code's manifest declares dependencies, and only Claude Code installs the missing ones.
Every other harness ignores the field, so the plugin installs and fails later with nothing to say
why. This reads what a plugin declares, checks it against what the running harness has installed and
enabled, and returns the steps that settle the rest. It installs nothing and compares no versions.

```ts
import { checkPluginDependencies, supportsPluginDependencies } from 'cyber-agentkit'

supportsPluginDependencies('claude-code') // true; false for the others

const check = await checkPluginDependencies('codex', { pluginRoot })
// {
//   harness: 'codex',
//   supported: false,
//   autoResolved: false,
//   dependencies: [{ name: 'my-dep', marketplace: 'my-marketplace', state: 'missing' }],
//   steps: ['…'],
//   research: ['E-DEP-2', …],
// }
```

`state` is `enabled`, `installed` (no explicit setting), `disabled`, `missing`, or `unknown` (the
harness keeps no readable install record). A dependency with no marketplace resolves only in the
declaring plugin's own marketplace, as Claude Code does, and is `unknown` when that marketplace
cannot be found.

`readPluginDependencies(pluginRoot)` reads the list from `extensions["io.github.cyber-uni.plugin-manager"]`
(or the older `extensions["org.cyberuni.universal-plugin"]`) in the root `plugin.json`, then from
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. `declaredPluginDependencies(manifest)` parses a manifest you already
hold. The how-to for a person or agent, `plugin-dependencies`, ships as a
[reference](#reference-documents).

## Skill directories

```ts
import { skillsDirectories } from 'cyber-agentkit'

skillsDirectories('claude-code') // { project: ['.claude/skills'], user: ['.claude/skills'], research: ['E-CC-L1'] }
skillsDirectories('codex')?.project.includes('.agents/skills') // true
```

## Headless runs

How to run a harness on one prompt with no user present: the command, the model and permission
flags, the output formats and where token usage and cost appear in them, the transcript location,
and the documented exit codes. The library only describes the run; starting the process is up to
you.

```ts
import { headlessCommand, headlessInvocation } from 'cyber-agentkit'

headlessCommand('claude-code', {
  prompt: 'Fix the failing test',
  model: 'sonnet',
  permission: 'unattended',
  outputFormat: 'stream-json',
})
// { executable: 'claude', args: ['-p', '--model', 'sonnet', '--permission-mode', 'bypassPermissions',
//   '--output-format', 'stream-json', '--verbose', 'Fix the failing test'] }

const codex = headlessInvocation('codex')
// codex.outputFormats[1]: { name: 'jsonl', args: ['--json'],
//   usage: { event: 'turn.completed', tokens: 'usage', accumulate: 'sum' } } (no dollar cost)

headlessInvocation('vscode-copilot').supported // false: no headless mode
headlessInvocation('opencode').supported // 'unknown': a one-shot mode exists, but its flags are not verified
```

Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Qwen Code are covered. `permission:
'unattended'` lets the run edit files and run commands without asking, so use it only in a
throwaway checkout. Exit codes are a weak signal: Claude Code documents only zero and non-zero, and
a run stopped by a turn or budget cap is told apart by the `result` message's `subtype`.

## Reference documents

A reference is a named Markdown document an agent reads on demand, such as a checklist or a set of
weights a skill applies. A plugin ships a contribution, a skill ships its default at
`<skill>/references/<name>.default.md`, and anyone can add their own without editing the plugin: a
repository in `.agents/references/<name>.md`, a person in `~/.agents/references/<name>.md`.

```ts
import { loadReference } from 'cyber-agentkit'

const resolved = await loadReference('agent-readiness-weights', {
	root: process.cwd(),
	// The plugin calling the resolver: its own `references/` is the first plugin layer.
	plugin: { name: 'my-plugin', root: pluginRoot },
	// The skill loading the name: its `references/<name>.default.md` joins as the default tier.
	defaultSkill: skillFolder,
})
if (resolved.status === 'found') console.log(resolved.content)
```

`status` is `found`, `missing`, `ambiguous` (nothing orders the plugins holding the name; pick one
of `resolved.options`, such as `my-plugin/agent-readiness-weights`, or settle it with
`reference customize --extends`), or `invalid` (not a reference name). A name not found also has a
`code`, such as `reference-missing`. `loadReference` never throws for a bad name. `warnings` holds each fault
as `{ code, message }`, and `trace` says how the document was built.

The tiers, highest first:

| Tier | Folders |
| --- | --- |
| managed | a `references/` beside the managed-policy files of the harness, read only when detection names exactly one harness |
| repo | `.agents/references/` at the repository root |
| user | `~/.agents/references/` |
| plugin | the calling plugin's `references/`, each plugin the harness has enabled, then each dependency in the root's `package.json` that has a plugin manifest, named by that manifest |
| default | `<skill folder>/references/<name>.default.md` of the skill loading the name |

The repository root is the nearest folder at or above the working folder that holds `.git` (a folder
or a file, so a git worktree counts), else the working folder. In each folder, only `<name>.md` and
`<name>/README.md` answer a name, in that order.

Contributions apply bottom first: the plugins and the default, in the order `extends` gives them,
then user, repo, and managed. Each applies over what is below it with its frontmatter `merge`:

- `patch` (the default): its sections replace the text they match by heading path, and the rest is
  kept.
- `combine`: its sections' text is added after the text they match, lower first; where combined text
  conflicts, the later text wins.
- `replace`: it replaces everything below.
- `remove`: it drops everything below.

A `<!-- merge: <operation> -->` marker under a heading applies an operation to that section alone.
Frontmatter `extends` lists what a contribution builds on, bottom first: plugins by their manifest
name, and `default`. The highest `extends` written in the managed, repo, or user tier builds the
stack; without one, the plugins' own `extends` order them. `resolved.metadata` holds the composed
frontmatter, the higher contribution winning each key, without `merge` and `extends`. Frontmatter
that is not a YAML mapping is ignored with a warning.

A `.agents/references/<name>.md` in a folder below the root, one that git does not ignore, is a
project section for that folder. It is not a tier. `load` delivers each one after the main document,
in path order, as `<project folder="...">...</project>` in text and as `projectSections` records in
structured output. The managed contribution applies over each section.

A plugin listed in the `package.json` of a folder below the root, and not already in the plugin tier,
adds a project section for that folder instead of a plugin layer: its own document for the name,
delivered ahead of the folder's own section and marked `plugin="..."` in text. So one package of a
monorepo can use a different plugin's version of a name, and the rest of the repository is unaffected.

A document written by `customize` from a request records its `sources` and `request`. `load` warns
`reference-stale` when a source plugin's version has changed since. A plugin or skill default can
list older names in `aliases`; a load of an older name resolves the new one with a
`reference-renamed` warning. An `extends` step's `sections` limits it to those top-level sections.
A reference that is not Markdown reads its description, tags, aliases, and picks from
`<name>.meta.md` beside it.

| Function | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `loadReference(name, options)` | Resolves one name for a root, with every tier read |
| `referenceLayers(options)` | Builds the ordered layers, and finds the skills holding a default, to resolve several names against |
| `resolveReference(name, layers)` | Resolves a name against layers |
| `listReferences(layers)`, `referenceNames(layers)` | Every name the layers hold, one row each, and a row per layer holding it |
| `listReferences(layers, { pattern })` | Every reference by exact name pattern |
| `searchReferences(query, layers)` | Names matching a query by name, description, heading, or body |
| `whereReference(name, layers, options)` | The files a customization is written to, what hides each, and the heading paths below |
| `createReference(options)`, `deleteReference(options)` | Start or delete a contribution; a plugin or skill source folder is `pluginFolder` or `default`, and `plugin` stays the host plugin |
| `customizeReference(options)` | Write the picks or a generated body for a name, as `reference customize` does; runs no model |
| `ReferenceError`, `referenceCodes` | The error a library function throws when it cannot complete, carrying a stable `code`, and the table of codes |
| `repoReferencesDir()`, `userReferencesDir()`, `defaultLayer()` | Single folders and layers |
| `declaredDependencies()`, `packageDir()`, `pluginManifestName()` | A manifest's declared packages, where each is installed, and a plugin's manifest name |
| `harnessSkillFolders()`, `pluginSkillFolders()`, `skillsIn()` | The skill folders a harness reads, and the skills in them, known by their `SKILL.md` name |
| `referenceImplementations(id, layers)` | The implementations of an interface a consumer can load, and those left out with why |
| `checkReferences(layers, options)` | Checks interface documents and their implementations, each as `load` composes it |

### The reference command

The package ships a `reference` command with `load`, `list`, `search`, `where`, `implementations`,
`check`, `create`, `customize`, and `delete` subcommands:

```sh
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference load <name>... --root <repository root> --default <skill folder>
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference list
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference list 'project-tracker.capabilities.*'
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference implementations <interface id> --accept 1,2
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference check
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference create <name> --merge combine
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference customize <name> --extends <plugin> --scope user
npx -y cyber-agentkit reference delete <name> --scope repo --dry-run
```

`implementations` lists what a consumer can load for an interface (a `<id>.interface` document) with
each one's pin, description, and unsupported sections. `check` verifies interface documents and
their implementations, and exits 0; failures are entries in the result's `failed` list.

`create`, `customize`, and `delete` act on `.agents/references/` at the root (`--scope repo`, the
default) or `~/.agents/references/` (`--scope user`), or on a folder's project section with
`--in <folder>`. `create` and `delete` also take `--plugin <plugin folder>` or
`--default <skill folder>` for a plugin's or a skill's source in the repository. `delete` reports
what answers the name afterwards, and never deletes a managed contribution or an installed copy.

`customize` runs no model. `--extends <step>...` writes the picks of what a name builds on, a step
being a plugin, `<plugin>:<merge>`, or `default`, and `--extends none` removes them. `--request <file>
--body <file>` writes a body a generator wrote, with the picks, sources, and request recorded;
`--implements <interface>` makes it a whole implementation; `--base` prints the input the generator
reads and writes nothing.

Output is [TOON](https://github.com/toon-format/toon) by default, for an agent to parse; pass
`--format json` or `--format text` (`load`, `create`, `customize`, and `delete` default to `text`).
Each command prints only the fields that answer it; on `load`, `--metadata` adds the status and the
composed frontmatter, and `--trace` adds how the document was built. Every warning carries a stable
`code`. A command that answered exits 0, including `load` for a name not found and `list`,
`search`, or `implementations` with nothing to show (an `empty:` message with `help` lines). A
command that could not complete exits 1, and a usage error exits 2; both print exactly one error
value on stdout, with `error`, `code`, any detail fields, and `help`, and write nothing to stderr.
In `text` a warning prints on stderr as `warning: <code>: <message>`; in `json` and `toon` it is in
the record's `warnings` list. A warning never changes the exit code. The formats
follow [`clibuilder`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/clibuilder) 12, and any other value is a
usage error (exit code 2). A CLI built on clibuilder 12
can host the same command under its own plugin name, imported from the `./commands` subpath. `--format`
is the host's global option, so the host's `cli({ format })` sets the default for every subcommand;
the `text` default of `load`, `create`, `customize`, and `delete` belongs to the `cyber-agentkit` CLI:

```ts
import { createReferenceCommand } from 'cyber-agentkit/commands'

app.command(createReferenceCommand({ plugin: { name: 'my-plugin', root: pluginRoot } }))
```

## Worktrees

The `./worktrees` subpath leases git worktrees to concurrent agent sessions, so two agents never
share a checkout. It does not fetch and never kills a process.

```ts
import { acquire, pruneWorktrees, release } from 'cyber-agentkit/worktrees'
```

| Function | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `acquire(options)` | Leases a worktree: recycles an idle one of its own, else creates one at the next free slot under `max` |
| `explain(options)` | Every worktree of the repository with the reason it cannot be reused, or none |
| `release()`, `claimLease()`, `holdsLease()` | The lease a holder takes on a worktree |
| `pruneWorktrees(options)` | Removes unleased, idle, clean, landed worktrees it owns. A dry run unless `apply` is set |
| `removeWorktree(options)` | Removes the one worktree you name, under the same safety checks |
| `seedWorktree(options)` | Copies the gitignored files a `.worktreeinclude` names into a new or recycled worktree |
| `listWorktrees()`, `occupants()`, `classifyOwner()` | The worktrees of a repository, the sessions working in each, and who owns each |

A worktree is skipped, with the reason in its verdict, when it is the primary checkout, owned by
another tool or person, leased, prunable, busy, dirty, or not yet landed on the default branch. The
checks fail closed: when git or the process probe cannot say, the worktree is left alone.

## Why this exists

`universal-plugin`, `buddy-agent-harness`, `repobuddy`, and `cyberlegion/cyber-mux` each need to know
which agent harness they are running under, and each was re-implementing that detection separately.
This package exists so they share one implementation instead.

# Asset

Lists, shows, creates, updates, and deletes the static files in a skill's `assets/` folder, such as templates, schemas, and JSON data a skill points to by path. By path: plain file operations with no tiers and no merging. By name: loads a file through the managed, project, user, and plugin tiers (the skill's own file is the default), so a plugin, the project, or the user can override which one a skill uses by placing its own. Nothing merges or extends. It runs the `asset` command from a launcher bundled in `scripts/`, and writes or deletes only after the user approves. Type `/asset` to run it yourself. Installed as a Claude Code plugin, it is `/cyber-agentkit:asset` (pnpm install: `pnpm-cyber-agentkit-asset`).

| Mode | When |
| --- | --- |
| list | see every file under the skill's `assets/` with its size |
| show | read a text asset |
| create | add a new asset; never overwrites. With `--copy`, start an override in the project or user tier as a copy of a plugin's, the default, or another tier's file (never managed) |
| update | replace an existing asset |
| delete | remove an asset and any folder it leaves empty |
| load, names, where, select | resolve an asset by name through the tiers, list names, show where an override goes, and choose which plugin's file answers a name several hold |

For a document fetched by name and layered across the managed, project, user, and plugin tiers, use [`/reference`](../reference/README.md).

# Update prose

Recommends updated prose for a section a tool wrote earlier and its owner may have edited. A caller hands over the offered prose, the found prose, and the historic prose (the wordings the tool retired). A script compares them sentence by sentence and returns, for each part, whether the found text is current, which retired wording it descends from, which sentences are the owner's, and the merged text or the exact sentences that collide. The skill reads those facts and resolves only what they leave open, marking every sentence it decided. It runs the `prose-update` command from a launcher bundled in `scripts/` and writes no file. Type `/prose-update` to run it yourself. Installed as a Claude Code plugin, it is `/cyber-agentkit:prose-update` (pnpm install: `pnpm-cyber-agentkit-prose-update`).

| Input | What |
| --- | --- |
| Offered prose | the wording the tool offers now |
| Found prose | the text in the file being updated |
| Historic prose | a history text of retired wordings, or one or more retired wordings, newest first |

| Outcome | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `up-to-date` | the found part already holds the offered wording |
| `update` | merged: the owner's sentences kept, the offered ones taken |
| `owners` | the part is the owner's own; nothing is offered |
| `conflict` | both sides changed the same sentences differently |
| `undetermined` | the facts do not settle it: no history, an empty section, a tied or missing base |

It ships in the `cyber-agentkit` plugin:

```text
/plugin marketplace add cyber-uni/marketplace
/plugin install cyber-agentkit@cyber-uni
```

# Reference

Loads, finds, inspects, creates, customizes, deletes, and migrates [references](https://cyber-uni.github.io/cyber-agentkit/concepts/reference-documents/): Markdown documents (or JSON, YAML, TOML, or text files, which are never merged) an agent reads on demand by name. It routes each request to the `reference` command, run from a launcher bundled in `scripts/`, and writes or deletes a reference only after the user approves it; a request to create one from text the user gives is that approval. Type `/reference` to run it yourself. Installed as a Claude Code plugin, it is `/cyber-agentkit:reference` (pnpm install: `pnpm-cyber-agentkit-reference`). Installed with pnpm, it is `pnpm-cyber-agentkit-reference`.

| Mode | When |
| --- | --- |
| Load | a skill's instructions name references, or an interface whose implementations, to load with this skill; it acts on each status and warning, and follows project sections for the folder the work is in |
| Find | `search` for a topic, `list` every reference, or `implementations` of an interface |
| Inspect | `load`; `load --trace` for how a name composed; `where` for the files a customization goes to; `check` against an interface |
| Create | writing a new reference from given text, for the repository, a folder, the user, a plugin (`<plugin name>.<reference>.md`), or a skill's default (`<name>.default.md`), or stubbing an interface; it shows where each section came from and offers the full document |
| Update | editing the user's own hand-written file in place |
| Customize | picking what a name builds on, changing its prose by request through a generator subagent, implementing an interface by request, or revising a stale generated document |
| Delete | removing a repo, user, or project-section contribution, saying first what answers the name afterwards |
| Migrate | rewriting files left in a version 1 form, and renaming files under a name a plugin renamed, with `migrate`; it shows the plan, calls out `user` files, and runs `migrate --write` only once the user approves |
| Wire a skill | giving a skill the line below |

It ships in the `cyber-agentkit` plugin:

```text

/plugin install cyber-agentkit@cyber-uni
```

# Skill

Designs an agent skill through aspects a team can swap one at a time. `/skill` creates a skill from a described job, checks it without running it, tests it by running its evals, fixes what check
or test found, enhances it beyond that, and customizes which implementation each aspect uses. Intent, Shape, and Trigger are built in. Criteria, Verification, and every
open aspect, such as Security, are references (`skill-design.aspects.<aspect>`) that another plugin can replace through
the `reference` skill's Customize mode. The default Verification runs each case several times in a sandbox, on
promptfoo, beside a run without the skill. Type `/skill` to run it yourself. Installed as a Claude Code plugin, it is
`/cyber-agentkit:skill` (pnpm install: `pnpm-cyber-agentkit-skill`).

| Command | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `help` | lists and explains the commands; also what a bare `/skill` shows |
| `create` | drafts Intent, Criteria, Shape, and Trigger for approval, builds the skill, then checks and tests it |
| `check` | reads the skill against every aspect; changes nothing |
| `test` | runs the evals and saves the result; changes nothing |
| `fix` | repairs what check or test found |
| `enhance` | suggests improvements one at a time, from use or a request |
| `customize` | shows which implementation each aspect uses and each command's autonomy, and changes them through the `reference` skill |

```text
/plugin install cyber-agentkit@cyber-uni
```

Type `/skillify` to run it yourself. Installed as a Claude Code plugin, it is `/cyber-agentkit:skillify` (pnpm install: `pnpm-cyber-agentkit-skillify`).
