## What a plugin declares

Only Claude Code's manifest declares dependencies: a `dependencies` array in `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` whose entries are `"name"`, `"name@marketplace"`, or `{ "name", "marketplace", "version" }` (E-DEP-1). A bare name resolves in the declaring plugin's own marketplace. A plugin can author the same list once in its root `plugin.json`, at `extensions["io.github.cyber-uni.plugin-manager"].dependencies` or, in plugins built before that key, `extensions["org.cyberuni.universal-plugin"].dependencies` (E-DEP-6 to E-DEP-8). Read it from there first, then from `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, whichever harness you run on.

## Check what is missing

Run the library's `checkPluginDependencies(harness, { pluginRoot })`. It reports each dependency as `enabled`, `installed` (no explicit setting), `disabled`, `missing`, or `unknown` (the harness keeps no readable install record), and returns the steps below that apply. It installs nothing.

## Claude Code

Claude Code resolves dependencies itself. `claude plugin install`, `/reload-plugins`, auto-update, and `marketplace add` install the missing ones, and a plugin whose dependency is missing or disabled does not load (E-DEP-2).

1. For a missing dependency, run `claude plugin install <name>@<marketplace>`.
2. For a disabled dependency, set its `<name>@<marketplace>` key to `true` in `enabledPlugins`.
3. Run `/reload-plugins`.

A dependency in another marketplace is not installed unless the root marketplace lists it in `allowCrossMarketplaceDependenciesOn`, or you already have it enabled. Without that, the install completes and the plugin then fails to load (E-DEP-3).

## Every other harness

`cursor`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `opencode`, `kilo`, `gemini-cli`, `qwen-code`, `vscode-copilot`, `cline`, `crush`, `openhands`, `augment` have no dependency field (E-DEP-4, E-DEP-5, E-CC-X1). Nothing is resolved for you, and no install command is given because none has been verified.

1. Read the dependencies as above.
2. Tell the user which marketplace each one needs. You cannot tell whether the harness has that marketplace added, so ask the user to check, and to add it if it is not.
3. Install each one through the harness's own plugin install flow, from its marketplace when one is named.
4. Enable each one.

# Create a reference

Create writes a new file from text the author gives, or an interface's stub. To change what an existing reference says in the customizer's own words, use Customize mode instead.

## 1. Check that it should be a reference

- If the agent must decide from the task that it needs this, it is a **skill**, not a reference. Say so and stop.
- If an `AGENTS.md` line, a skill, or a person will name it, it is a reference. Continue.

## 2. Choose where it lives

| Who it is for | Where | Flag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| everyone working in this repository | `.agents/references/<name>.md` at the root | (none) |
| work in one folder of the repository | `<folder>/.agents/references/<name>.md` | `--in <folder>` |
| the user, in every repository | `~/.agents/references/<name>.md` | `--scope user` |
| every user of a plugin | `references/<name>.md` in the plugin's source folder | `--plugin <plugin folder>` |
| a skill, as its default | `references/<name>.default.md` in the skill's source folder | `--default <skill folder>` |

`--plugin` and `--default` write only into a source folder in this repository, never into an installed copy. A folder's project section states only what differs there, and takes no `--merge`.

## 3. Name it

- Use lowercase words joined by `-`. A name is a file name, never a path, and never ends `.default`.
- **A plugin prefixes every name it ships** with its own name and a dot: `cyber-asana.work-hierarchy`, not `work-hierarchy`. A repository's or user's own reference needs no prefix. A skill's default takes the name its skill loads.
- **An implementation of an interface takes the interface's id as its namespace**: `<id>` when the interface's cardinality is `one`, `<id>.<key>` when it is `many`. Read the interface with `load <id>.interface`.
- Run `load <name>`. If the name already resolves and the author wants a new document, pick another name. To change the existing one, go to Customize mode.
- When a plugin or a skill renames a name it ships, list the old name in the new file's `aliases` frontmatter, so load lines and customizations written for the old name still reach it.
- When a plain reference becomes the interface document of a `many` interface, list its old name in the interface document's `aliases` the same way. For a `one` interface, add the rename to the plugin's `references/_renames.yaml` instead.

## 4. Write it

A reference is top-level `##` sections, with no single `#` title holding them, and a `description` in its frontmatter:

```md
---
description: One line that says what the reference covers.
tags: [testing, fixtures]
---

## Fixtures

Instructions only.
```

- `description` and `tags` are what `search` matches. Always write a `description`.
- If the author's text starts with a `#` title, drop the title and make the sections under it top-level `##` sections.
- Write instructions an agent follows. Leave the rationale out.

Run `create`; never write the file by hand:

1. Run `create <name> --dry-run`, with the flag from step 2. Add `--template <path>` with the file holding the author's text; without it, the command writes its own template. Add `--merge <operation>` when it should not patch: `combine` to add after what is below, `replace` to stand alone, `remove` to turn the name off.
2. When the request gave the text, the request is the approval: run the same command without `--dry-run`, then show the author the path, the content, and any `hint:` or `warning:` line. A warning that a contribution above hides the file still writes it.
3. Otherwise, show the author the path, the content it printed, and any `hint:` or `warning:` line, and on approval run the same command without `--dry-run`.

If `create` refuses, report its reason and write nothing. An existing file with a body means Customize mode, or Update mode for a file the user wrote by hand.

A plugin's file or a skill's default that changes how another plugin's reference reads, such as a house style, lists `extends: [<other plugin>]` in its frontmatter and holds only the sections it changes. `create` records in `sources` the version of each plugin it extends, so `check` warns the author when that plugin moves on. Never give such a file `merge: replace`; `create` refuses it.

## 5. Stub an interface

Run `create <name> --implements <id> --dry-run` instead of passing a template. It writes each section of the interface as a `##` heading, stubbed `**Unsupported.**` with what the section holds, and sets `implements: <id>@<version>` and `merge: replace`. With `--in <folder>`, it writes a project section with neither. Show it, write it on approval, then replace each stub with the section, or keep `**Unsupported.**` followed by one sentence on why. A required section cannot stay unsupported. Run `check <name>`; it must pass.

## 6. Show the result

1. Run `load <name> --trace`, adding `--default <skill folder>` for a skill's default. The new file must be `used`, or the trace names what hides it.
2. Show the author where each section came from: for each row of the trace's `sections`, the heading and the contributions that built it.
3. Offer the full document. When the author accepts, run `load <name>` and show what it prints.

For a plugin reference, run the command where the plugin is installed; otherwise, say that the plugin tier was not checked.

## 7. Connect it to a caller

Nothing loads a reference by itself. Tell the author where to name it:

- For a repository, add a line to `AGENTS.md`, or to the skill that needs it, such as: "Read the `testing` reference before writing tests."
- For a plugin or a skill's default, add the load line to each skill that needs it, as Wire a skill says.

# Customize a reference

Customize changes what a skill reads for a name, for the repository, for the user alone, or for one folder. The customizer picks what the name builds on, says in their own words what to change in the prose, or both. The `customize` command writes the file and its record and runs no model; you run the generator.

With no user present, write nothing. When the command cannot run, write nothing and say so.

## 1. Read what the name is now

1. Run `load <name> --trace`. Add `--default <skill folder>` when a skill loads the name, and use it in every command below.
2. Note the status, the stack, and each `repo`, `user`, or project-section layer. A layer that records a `request` is generated. A layer whose outcome is `stale` goes to [Revise a stale document](#5-revise-a-stale-document).

## 2. Choose the target

Ask who the change is for, and use that target's flags in every command below:

| Who it is for | Flags |
| --- | --- |
| everyone working in this repository | (none) |
| only the user, in every repository | `--scope user` |
| work in one folder of the repository | `--in <folder>` |

Run `where <name>` with those flags. Tell the customizer the file it writes, who it reaches, and what hides it. A hidden target is still written, with a warning.

## 3. Pick what it builds on

Skip this step for `--in <folder>`: a project section takes no picks.

1. The options are the plugins that hold the name, each `<plugin>/<name>`, and `default` when a skill has one. An ambiguous name lists them in its `options`.
2. Ask the customizer which to build on, bottom first, even when only one is left.
3. Run `customize <name> --extends <step>... --dry-run` with the target's flags. A step is a plugin's name, `<plugin>:<merge>` (such as `house-style:combine`), or `default`. For steps that contribute only some sections, write the whole `extends` list to a YAML file and pass `--extends-file <file>`. To remove the picks, pass `--extends none`.
   To pick for every interface of a family at once, such as the aspects of one skill, give the family `<prefix>.*` as the name with the same `--extends` steps and no `sections`. Each `one` interface a step can answer gets the picks; one no step holds keeps what it had, and a `many` one is skipped; the result names both.
4. Show the path and the content. On approval, run it without `--dry-run`.

The picks record, as `declined`, every plugin holding the name that they leave out, so load stops asking about it. When load warns `plugin-not-selected` about a plugin installed later, ask the customizer whether to add it to the picks or leave it out; to leave it out, write the same picks again.

Picks alone write a selection, or change only `extends` on a file that has a body. When that body records a request, the output suggests customizing again with it: offer step 4.

## 4. Change the prose by request

1. If the name is ambiguous, do step 3 first. Write the customizer's request, in their own words, to a temporary file.
2. Run `customize <name> --base` with the target's flags and any new `--extends` picks. It prints what the generator reads, and writes nothing. It leaves out the target file, managed text, the tier above the target, and personal text.
3. Spawn a generator subagent. Give it the prompt in [The generator](#the-generator), the printed base, and the request. Say whether to write a delta (the default) or a whole document (the customizer asked to replace everything). If you cannot spawn a subagent, follow that prompt yourself, reading only the base and the request.
4. Write the draft to a temporary file. Run `customize <name> --request <request file> --body <draft file> --dry-run` with the target's flags, adding `--merge replace` for a whole document.
5. Show the customizer the path and the draft. If they decline, write nothing. If they change the request, start this step again with the new request.
6. Only after they approve, run the same command without `--dry-run`.
7. Run `load <name> --trace`. The written file must be `used`, or the trace names what hides it.

If `customize` refuses with `body-not-generated`, the target holds a body written by hand. Offer Update mode, or deleting it first.

### Implement an interface by request

To implement an interface for the name, add `--implements <id>` to the `--base` and to the write. The base then starts with the interface's stub. The draft is a whole document that holds every section of the interface, in its order. With `--in <folder>`, it is a project section for that folder alone, so one package can implement the interface its own way. After the write, run `check <name>`; it must pass.

A name that is `missing` under a found interface's namespace needs `--implements <id>`; `customize` refuses it otherwise and says how to name the interface.

## 5. Revise a stale document

Load reports a generated document `stale` when a plugin it was built from changed or is gone. Revise it from its recorded request; the customizer does not restate it.

1. From `load <name> --trace`, read the stale layer's `request`, its picks (`extends` in its `frontmatter`), and its `sources`.
2. If a source's status is `missing`, its plugin is gone. Tell the customizer before you generate anything. They pick again (step 3), or go on without it.
3. Revise the main document first: the `repo` or `user` document. Then revise each stale project section, one at a time, with `--in <folder>`. Each project section records the main document it was written against.
4. For each one, write its recorded request to a file and follow step 4 with the same target. The recorded picks apply unless the customizer picked again. The base never holds the stale document, so the request is not applied over its own earlier result.
5. A JSON, YAML, TOML, or text document is regenerated whole.

If the customizer declines, write nothing; the document stays stale.

## The generator

Give the generator subagent this prompt, followed by the base and the request:

> You write one reference document for the `reference` skill of `cyber-agentkit`. You get a base document and a customizer's request.
>
> - Apply the request to the base. Change only what the request asks for.
> - Write one concise document of instructions an agent follows. Leave out rationale and history.
> - Keep every heading path you use exactly as the base has it, so later loads match it. Add a new section only when the request needs one.
> - For a delta (the default), write only the sections you change, each under its heading path from the base. To drop a section, write its heading followed by `<!-- merge: remove -->`.
> - For a whole document, write every section, in the base's order.
> - For a project section, write only what differs for work in that folder.
> - For an interface, keep every section of the stub, in its order. Replace each stub with its content, or keep `**Unsupported.**` with one sentence on why. A required section cannot stay unsupported.
> - Use top-level `##` sections and no `#` title. Write no frontmatter; the command records it.
> - Use only the base and the request. Never add text from anywhere else, such as managed or admin instructions, or other files you can see.
> - Reply with the document alone.

# Load references for a caller

Load the references a calling skill names, and hand them back as part of its instructions. The **caller** is the skill whose instructions sent you here; its **folder** is the directory its `SKILL.md` is in.

When the caller names an interface ("Load the implementations of the `<id>` interface"), follow [Implementations of an interface](#implementations-of-an-interface) for it. Load any names it also lists with steps 1 to 6.

## 1. Run the command once

Find the caller's folder from what the harness told you when the caller loaded: a `Base directory for this skill: <folder>` line, or the path of its `SKILL.md`. Collect every name the caller listed, in its order, and run one command for all of them:

```sh
node <this skill's folder>/scripts/reference.mjs load <name>... --default <caller folder>
```

- `<this skill's folder>` is the directory the `reference` skill's `SKILL.md` is in.
- `--default <caller folder>` adds the caller's own defaults below every other contribution.
- Add `--root <repository root>` only when the working folder is not in the repository you work in.
- When you cannot tell the caller's folder, leave out `--default`. The names then load without the caller's defaults. Tell the user so in step 5.
- Never use `npx`, `pnpm dlx`, `upx`, or any other package runner, and never download anything, not even when this command cannot run. Go to step 4 instead.

Do not read `.agents/references/`, `~/.agents/`, any plugin's `references/`, or the caller's `references/` yourself. What answers a name is the command's decision.

## 2. Read the result

The result is on stdout. One found name prints its document. Several print each as `<reference name="…">` … `</reference>`, in the order asked. A name that was not found prints `<reference name="…" status="…" code="…">message</reference>` in its place, also when it is the only name. Read the status and the code from that tag. The command exits 0 even when a name was not found.

A found document may end with project sections, each wrapped as `<project folder="…">` … `</project>`. Each one states what differs for work in that folder. A section marked `plugin="…"` comes from a plugin that folder's `package.json` lists.

A warning prints on stderr as `warning: <code>: <message>`. It does not change the answer.

**The command ran** when every name you asked for appears on stdout as a document or a status tag. Exit 1 or 2 with one error value on stdout (`error:` and `code:` lines) means it ran but could not answer: go to step 4 and report the error. Anything else (`Cannot find module`, `node: not found`, a stack trace, no mention of the names) means it did not run: go to step 4.

## 3. Act on each name

- **found**: use the document.
- **missing** with `reference-missing`: carry on without it, and tell the user it was not loaded. Do not read the caller's default or search for a substitute: the command already included the default.
- **missing** with `reference-removed`: a `remove` turned the name off on purpose. Carry on without it, and say nothing about it. It is not a fault.
- **ambiguous** with `reference-ambiguous`: more than one plugin holds the name and nothing says which to build on. The tag ends with `; options: …`: each `<plugin>/<name>`, and `default` when the caller has one.
  - With a user present, list every option, including `default`, even when only one is left. Ask which the name should build on, and whether the pick is for the repository (the default) or only for them. Write the pick with `reference customize <name> --extends <step>`, where the step is the option's plugin part or `default`, adding `--default <caller folder>`, and `--scope user` when it is for them only. Then run step 1 again for that name alone and use what it prints.
  - With no user present, carry on without it, and tell the user to settle it with Customize mode.
- **invalid** with `reference-invalid`: the caller's load line names something that is not a reference name. Never read the path or file it names. Carry on without it, and tell the user it is a fault in the caller's instructions, to report to the caller's author.

Pass every warning on to the user, one line each, and use the reference as loaded. A `reference-stale` warning means a generated document was built against plugins that have since changed: name the changed plugins from its message, and say that Customize mode revises the document from its recorded request. A `plugin-not-selected` warning means a plugin installed after the customizer picked what the name builds on also holds it, and is not used: name the plugin, and say that Customize mode adds it, or leaves it out so the warning stops. A `reference-legacy-format` warning means a file is in a form version 1 wrote, and a `reference-renamed` warning that names a plugin's rename means a file sits under a name the plugin renamed: name the file, and say that Migrate mode updates it. A warning about an installed plugin's file is for that plugin's author; say so.

## 4. When the command did not run

Read the caller's default of every name, and only then. Never read a default for a name the command reported, whatever its status. A name's default is the first of these in the caller's folder:

1. `references/<name>.default.md`
2. `references/<name>.default.json`, `.default.yaml`, `.default.yml`, `.default.toml`, then `.default.txt`

A name with no such file is not loaded. Never read `references/<name>.md`; it is not a default.

## 5. Report

Tell the user, briefly:

- each name not loaded, and why: missing, ambiguous (with the options), or invalid (a fault for the caller's author). Leave out a name a `remove` turned off.
- each warning, one line each.
- when the command did not run: that it did not, the error it gave, and that each name came from the caller's default, so no managed text, project section, or repository or user customization applied. When a name has no default, add that `scripts/reference.mjs` ships with the npm package, so a `cyber-agentkit` plugin installed from git has none, and installing it from npm fixes it.
- when you could not tell the caller's folder: that the names loaded without its defaults.

Say nothing about the load when every name was found with no warning.

## 6. Follow the references

Return to the caller. Follow each loaded document as part of its instructions. Carry on without a name that was not loaded.

Where instructions conflict, follow them in this order, highest first:

1. company and team instructions the harness gives you;
2. a single feature's own document the caller points you at;
3. the resolved reference, or the default read when the command did not run.

Within a resolved reference, the project section for the folder the work is in ranks over the main document. When sections of nested folders both apply, follow both, and the inner folder's section wins where they conflict. When one folder has a section marked `plugin="…"` and one without, follow both, and the one without wins where they conflict. Managed text needs no ranking: the command already applied it.

Follow a project section whenever your work is in its folder. When the work moves into a folder partway through the task, follow that folder's project section from then on, without loading again. Stop following it when the work leaves the folder.

## Implementations of an interface

1. Run:

   ```sh
   node <this skill's folder>/scripts/reference.mjs implementations <id> --trace --format json
   ```

   Add `--accept <versions>`, such as `--accept 1,2`, when the caller names the interface versions it knows. The rules of step 1 apply: add `--root` only outside the repository, no package runner, no download, and no reading tier folders yourself.
2. Exit 0 prints one JSON object. `implementations` lists each one the caller can load, with its `pin`, `description`, and the `unsupported` sections it does not honor. It is empty when there are none. `excluded` lists each one left out, with its `reasons`. An unknown interface exits 1 with one error value on stdout, code `interface-unknown`; then the interface is not loaded.
3. Hand the list to the caller. The caller picks the implementations it needs; load each by its `pin` with steps 1 to 6.
4. Tell the user, briefly, about each excluded implementation and its reasons, and about an interface not loaded and its error.

## Validate

Before returning to the caller:

- Every name the caller listed is loaded from the command, read from the caller's default because the command did not run, or named in the report as not loaded.
- The caller's default was read only when the command did not run, never for a name the command reported.
- An ambiguous name was written with `reference customize --extends` only after the user picked an option and a scope.
- Every warning was passed on, one line each.
- No `npx`, `pnpm dlx`, `upx`, or download was run.
- No file under a tier folder, and no path an invalid name gives, was read by you.

# Check a skill

Read the skill against every aspect without running it. Change no file, and run no part of the skill.

## 1. Find it

Take a path, or a name looked up in the repository's and the user's skills folders. If it cannot be found, stop and
say where you looked.

## 2. Run the script checks

Run `check <skill folder> --format json` as `SKILL.md`'s Run the command says. It reports the Agent Skills
specification checks and every `script` check of the chosen implementations, running each one's check script, and
lists the rest as not checked. It exits 1 when a check fails. When no form of the command can run, decide the `script`
checks yourself by reading the files. The same command runs in CI.

## 3. Decide the rest

For each aspect, core and open, decide each `read` check by reading the skill. Report each `run` check as not checked,
pointing to `test`, never as a pass. A skill that fails the Agent Skills specification still gets every aspect checked.

## Report

One line per aspect: pass, fail, or not checked. Under each fail, the check's ID, its statement, and the part of the
skill that breaks it, quoted with its file. In an interactive run with failures, offer `fix`.

# Create a skill

Build a new skill for a job the author describes, one core aspect at a time.

## 1. Place it

1. Ask where the skill goes, unless the author said: the repository's skills folder (`.agents/skills/` when the
   repository has one), a plugin's `skills/`, or the user's own skills folder.
2. Propose a name: lowercase words joined by `-`, naming the job.
3. If `<place>/<name>/SKILL.md` already exists, stop, change nothing, and point to `check`, `fix`, and `enhance`.

## 2. Walk the core aspects

Load the aspects as `SKILL.md` says. For each of Intent, Criteria, Shape, and Trigger, in that order:

1. Draft the aspect as its Draft says, from the description and the aspects approved before it.
2. At `ask` (the default for `create`), show the draft and ask the author to approve it. Write nothing before they
   do. At `apply-safe` or `apply`, write it and report it.
3. Write the approved part into `<place>/<name>/`. A skill stopped partway keeps every approved part on disk.

When the author rejects a draft, redraft that aspect, and reopen every aspect after it that was already approved.

## 3. Build the skill

Write the approved Intent as the opening of `README.md`. Write the steps of `SKILL.md` before `## Done when`: the instructions an agent follows to do the job
and meet each criterion. Follow the approved Shape. Then check the result against the Agent Skills rules in
`SKILL.md`'s Rules.

## 4. Verify

1. Draft the Verification aspect as its Draft says, from the approved Criteria and the Trigger's near misses, and get
   it approved as in step 2.
2. Run [check](check.md), then [test](test.md).
3. When `test` fails, leave the skill in place, report each failing criterion, and offer `fix`.

## Report

The skill's path, each aspect approved, the `check` result, and the `test` result per criterion.

# Customize the aspects and autonomy

Show what `/skill` uses, take the author's picks in one answer, and write them through the `reference` skill of
`cyber-agentkit`. Write no reference file yourself.

## 1. Show what is in use

1. With the `reference` skill's Find mode, run `implementations skill-design.aspects.*`. For each aspect, show the
   implementation in use (`inUse`) and the ones available, each with its pin and description.
2. Load `skill-design.autonomy` and show each command's level (`ask`, `apply-safe`, or `apply`).
3. With an `[aspect]` given, show only that aspect, and say the others are unchanged.

## 2. Ask once

Ask in one question what to change: an implementation per aspect, one plugin for every aspect, autonomy levels, and
whether it applies to the whole repository (`repo`, the default) or to the author alone (`user`). Change nothing the
author does not name.

## 3. Write through `reference`

With the `reference` skill's Customize mode:

- One plugin for every aspect: one `customize skill-design.aspects.*` with that plugin as the step.
- A pick per aspect: one `customize skill-design.aspects.<aspect>` per aspect named.
- Autonomy: customize `skill-design.autonomy` with the levels asked, by request; it is not part of the aspect family.

## Report

Each aspect and level: what it uses now, and for each one not changed, why (the plugin does not implement it, or the
author did not name it). Say that the next `/skill` command uses the new picks.

# Enhance a skill

Suggest what would make a skill that passes `check` better, one suggestion at a time.

## 1. Start

1. Find the skill as [check](check.md) does. If the prompt names evidence that cannot be read, stop and name it.
2. Run `check`. When it fails, point to `fix`, and go on only if the author says so; with no author present, stop.
3. When the prompt asks for a different job from the skill's Intent, say so, point to `create`, and change nothing.

## 2. Gather evidence

The evidence is this session by default, or what the prompt points to: past transcripts, the harness's memory, a
saved `test` result. Read only what the harness already records. Note where each lesson appears: a lesson from use is
offered only once it has happened at least twice across everything read. A saved `test` result counts as one
occurrence of each pattern it shows, such as a criterion that passes in the baseline too. A rubric that failed a result
meeting its criterion, or passed one that does not, is a fault in the evals, not a lesson: offer the rubric change from
a single occurrence. Evidence that points at another skill, or at
no skill, changes nothing; say where it points.

## 3. Suggest

Review the skill against every aspect, core and open, using each aspect's Enhance, the evidence, and the prompt. For
each suggestion give the change, the aspect it touches, the reason, and the evidence it came from. Leave out any change
the skill already has, and any the author declined before for this skill.

- A trigger miss becomes a new trigger case; a wrong result becomes a new outcome case.
- A change to a core aspect reopens every core aspect after it.

## 4. Apply

At `ask` (the default), offer each suggestion on its own; the answer to one decides nothing about the others. Write only
accepted ones. With no author present, apply a suggestion only when the level allows it and `test` shows no criterion
worse than the skill's expected result, or, with none, the last saved result; when `test` cannot run, apply nothing. Never edit a skill from an installed plugin from
evidence of use: leave the suggestion for the author to send upstream.

After writing, run `check`; it passes, or [fix](fix.md)'s rule for a check that a change broke applies.
When a written change touches the skill's steps, its Criteria, or its evals, offer to run `test`, saying it makes
model calls and what the last run cost. When the result shows no criterion worse than before, offer to keep it as the
skill's expected result with `skill accept <folder>`.

## Report

Each suggestion with its outcome: applied, declined, or left for the author with its evidence. With nothing to suggest,
say so and change nothing.

# Fix a skill

Repair what `check` or `test` found, and nothing else.

## 1. Get the failures

Use the latest `check` or `test` result in this session, or the saved `test` result (the last one `test` saved, not the expected result). With neither, run [check](check.md),
and run [test](test.md) only when the author asks. With no failures, say there is nothing to fix and change nothing.

## 2. Repair each one

1. If the skill came from an installed plugin, say before the first edit that a plugin update will overwrite it.
2. For each failure, apply its aspect's Fix. Change only the part the failure named.
3. A repair that needs the author's decision, such as a new Intent, is asked; with no author present, report it as not
   repaired.
4. At `apply-safe` (the default for `fix`), keep a repair only when the failed check now passes and no other check
   fails; ask about the rest.
5. When a repair makes another check fail, show both to the author, who keeps it, undoes it, or asks for another
   repair. With no author present, undo it and report both.

## 3. Check again

Run the failed checks again. For a skill from an installed plugin, offer to file an issue with the plugin's source;
with no author present, file none.

## Report

Each failure: repaired, with the change, or not repaired, with the reason; and the result of the checks run again.

# Help

Show this list, then ask which command the author wants. Run no script and change no file.

| Command | Does | Use it when | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `help` | lists these commands | you do not know which command fits | `/skill help` |
| `create [description]` | drafts Intent, Criteria, Shape, and Trigger for approval, builds the skill, then checks and tests it | you want a new skill for a job you describe | `/skill create a skill that drafts release notes from merged PRs` |
| `check [skill]` | reads the skill against every aspect's checks, like a linter; changes nothing | you want to know whether a skill as written is sound, without running it | `/skill check release-notes` |
| `test [skill]` | runs the skill's evals: does it fire on the right requests, and does its result meet its Criteria | you want evidence the skill works, beside a run without it | `/skill test release-notes` |
| `fix [skill]` | repairs what `check` or `test` found, and nothing else | `check` or `test` reported failures | `/skill fix release-notes` |
| `enhance [skill] [prompt]` | suggests improvements one at a time, from how the skill was used or your request | the skill passes `check`, and you want it better | `/skill enhance release-notes it misses squash merges` |
| `customize [aspect]` | shows which implementation each aspect uses and each command's autonomy, and changes them | your team wants another plugin's checks, or commands to apply more or less on their own | `/skill customize verification` |

To turn work already done (a session, existing instructions, another skill) into a skill, use `/skillify`.

# Test a skill

Run the skill's evals, as the Verification aspect says. Change no file of the skill, except the expected result when
the author asks to accept one, or when the first passing run saves one (see Save the result).

## 1. Find it and its cases

1. Find the skill as [check](check.md) does.
2. If the skill has no `## Done when`, report every outcome as not tested, pointing to `check` and `fix`; trigger
   cases still run.
3. If it has no eval cases, draft them as Verification's Draft says and get the author's approval before any run. With
   no author present, run nothing and report the missing cases.
4. A criterion with no rubric is reported as not tested, pointing to `fix`.

## 2. Run

Run the cases as Verification's Run says. Pass a judge only when the author named one. A case marked as having an
outside effect is not run, and is reported as such.

A full test makes many runs and can take several minutes. Before starting, tell the author how many runs it makes
and, from the plan line, about how long and how much it took last time. Start it in the background where the harness
can, so the author can keep working, and watch its progress lines on stderr: one per finished run (`[n/total] <case>
run <k> (<arm>): <outcome>`) and a `still running` line when none has finished for 30 seconds. Pass them on at most once
a minute, in one short update that sums up the lines since the last one: the count so far (`n/total`), each run with
the skill that failed or was not run, and the latest `still running` line when no run finished. Send nothing when no
line has come since the last update. A run without the skill that fails is the baseline doing worse, not news. Never
quote the model's replies in an update.

## 3. Save the result

The result goes to `.agents/skill-design/results/<skill name>/latest.json` at the repository root (or under `~/` when
the skill is outside a repository), after the previous `latest.json` moves to `<its at>.json` beside it. The results
folder holds a `.gitignore` containing `*`, so each run's result stays local and out of version control. Each save keeps
`latest.json` and the 5 most recent past results of that skill, and deletes older ones. The result records the skill's
absolute folder as `folder`. Each save also deletes the results folder of any other skill under the same results folder
whose `latest.json` names a `folder` that no longer exists, so throwaway skills leave nothing behind; a results folder
whose `latest.json` has no `folder` or cannot be read is left alone, and nothing outside the results folder, nor any
`evals/expected.json`, is ever deleted. The default Verification's command saves it; another implementation writes the same shape:

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "skill": "release-notes",
  "folder": "/home/me/code/app/skills/release-notes",
  "at": "2026-11-10T21:00:00Z",
  "verification": "skill-design.aspects.verification from cyber-agentkit",
  "runs": 3,
  "threshold": 2,
  "baseline": "without the skill",
  "trigger": [
    { "case": "trigger-1", "prompt": "write release notes", "expect": "fire", "fired": 3, "ran": 3, "status": "pass" }
  ],
  "criteria": [
    {
      "id": "C2",
      "status": "fail",
      "passed": 1,
      "ran": 3,
      "baseline": { "passed": 0, "ran": 3 },
      "failures": [{ "case": "two-prs", "run": 2, "output": "Merge pull request #12" }]
    }
  ],
  "cases": [
    { "case": "trigger-1", "status": "pass" },
    { "case": "two-prs", "status": "fail" }
  ],
  "notRun": [{ "case": "post-to-github", "reason": "outside effect" }],
  "comparedWith": "expected",
  "changed": [{ "case": "two-prs", "from": "pass", "to": "fail" }],
  "cost": 0.06,
  "durationMs": 252000
}
```

`status` is `pass`, `fail`, `not-tested` (with a `reason`), or `not-run` (with a `reason`). A run that errors or hits a
limit is in `notRun` and never counts as a pass. When the baseline cannot run, `baseline` holds the reason and no
criterion has a `baseline` field.

`cases` holds each case's status: an outcome case passes when every criterion it tests meets the threshold in it.
`changed` lists the cases that went between `pass` and `fail` since the skill's expected result
(`<skill folder>/evals/expected.json`) when it exists, else since the previous saved result; `comparedWith` says which
(`expected` or `previous`). With neither, `changed` is left out and `noPrevious` is `true`. `cost` is the runs' total in US dollars, when the engine reports it.

### Accept a result

When the skill has no expected result yet and every case and criterion passes, `skill test` saves that result as the
expected one and its report carries `savedAsExpected: true`: tell the author it was saved. A first run with a fail saves
none. Otherwise only the author's request makes a result the expected result, and nothing else writes into the skill's
folder. `skill test <folder> --accept` runs the test as usual, then writes that result to `<skill folder>/evals/expected.json`,
in the same shape as `latest.json` but without `folder`, since the file is committed. `skill accept <folder>` writes the last saved result there without running the
test, so it spends nothing, and fails with `no-result` when there is none saved. The expected result is kept in version
control with the skill, so the team compares with the same result.

## Report

Each trigger case beside what was expected; each criterion's pass rate, threshold, and baseline; each failure with its
case and the output that broke it; and the cases that changed between pass and fail since the expected result, or, with
none, the previous result, saying which. With neither, say there is none to compare. Say when the result was saved as the
expected result. In an interactive run with failures, offer `fix`.
